questions.question: A student writes v = u + at² for final velocity. Show how dimensional analysis rejects it instantly.
questions.solution: [v] = LT⁻¹, but [at²] = LT⁻²·T² = L. A length cannot be added to a velocity — dimensions must match on both sides of any physical equation. The check can't prove a formula RIGHT (a dimensionally correct formula may still be wrong), but it reliably kills wrong ones.

questions.question: Two students measure a wire's length as 10.02, 10.03, 10.01 cm and 10.45, 9.55, 10.5 cm. Both average near 10.02 cm. Who is more accurate, who more precise?
questions.solution: Student 1 is precise (readings cluster tightly) AND accurate (cluster sits on the true value). Student 2's readings scatter widely — imprecise — though their mean may land near truth, which is luck, not skill. Precision = repeatability (spread); accuracy = closeness to the true value.

questions.question: Why is (2.5 m) × (3.42 m) reported as 8.6 m² and not 8.55 m²?
questions.solution: The result cannot be more reliable than its weakest input: 2.5 has 2 significant figures, so the answer is rounded to 2 s.f. — 8.6 m². Carrying the calculator's extra digits claims a precision the measurement never had. Rule: multiply/divide → fewest s.f.; add/subtract → fewest decimal places.

questions.question: Why are only 7 quantities (length, mass, time, etc.) chosen as fundamental, and how does force end up derived from three of them?
questions.solution: Fundamental quantities are a minimal independent set — none can be defined from the others; every other quantity is built from them. Force = mass × acceleration = [M][LT⁻²] = MLT⁻², built from mass, length, time. The set is chosen for independence and measurability, not because nature 'has only 7'.

questions.question: A stopwatch consistently runs 0.2 s slow. Repeating the measurement 50 times — does that fix it? Distinguish the two error types.
questions.solution: No — that is a SYSTEMATIC error: it shifts every reading the same way, and repetition cannot remove it (it needs calibration). Random errors scatter both ways, so averaging many readings reduces them. Fix systematic by calibrating; reduce random by averaging.
